The leased job (lease hvli:privacy:retention-purge) checks every hour and runs once the Oslo date has reached that day of the current academic year while the audit log holds no completed real run for the year that ended, so a server that is down on the day purges at its first check after. The CLI (privacy/purge/purgeCli.ts) refuses a real run before that day; its dry run runs on any day. Added 2026-11-05 (integration): config/env.ts declares PURGE_RUN_DATE, so a value outside those days stops the start-up by name (test/config/purgeEnv.test.ts); before, an unknown variable was dropped and the default applied. Operations run the CLI as npm run --silent privacy:purge -- --dry-run|--execute from apps/server.
    • Which rows: every row whose stored academicYear is before the current academic year, not only the year that just ended, so a year that a missed run left behind goes too; a row of the current year is never selected. Then the learner Identity rows created before the current academic year began (the moment the ended year ended), then the learner User rows left without an Identity that were created before that moment and own no activity. Amends D-034's consequence: a learner account created in the current year and left without an identity (its platform removed, say) stays until the next purge, because the purge leaves everything of the current year alone; such a row holds an ID, a kind and a time only. (AccountResolver writes a new user and its identity in one nested create, one transaction, so no purge can find one without the other; the rule is about the year, not a race.) Corrected 2026-11-04 (step 5 review): this sentence first gave such a race as the reason.
    • Order and batches: the snapshots first, then GradeSyncJob, XapiStatement, H5PUserData, Identity and User, each in transactions of at most 1 000 rows, so a large year neither locks a table for long nor is held in memory. A run that fails part-way keeps its snapshots and what it deleted; the next run deletes the rest. A table is done only when a page of its rows comes back empty or short: a batch that deletes fewer rows than it found (another writer took them meanwhile: an activity deleted with its statements, a state reset, a data-subject erasure, a second run) does not end it, since a run that ended early would be audited as completed and the job would leave the rest for a year. The same page found twice with nothing deleted fails the run (audited, retried at the next check) instead of looping. Added 2026-11-04 (step 5 review): the first version stopped a table at a batch that deleted nothing. Added 2026-11-04 (second step 5 review): each batch's delete repeats the filter its page was read with, so a row that stopped matching in between stays: a learner whom a login made staff after the page was read and before its delete (AccountResolver changes the kind of the account it found) keeps their identity, so their staff account is not left without one. The first version deleted a page's identities by their IDs alone. Added 2026-11-05 (integration): the other side of that race is closed in AccountResolver. A login that found an identity makes its account staff only while that identity still exists, in one statement (UPDATE with an EXISTS on the identity); if the purge removed it in between, or before the key rotation's re-hash, the login finds nothing and creates a new account, as for a first login. The old learner account, now without an identity, is left to the next purge, so no staff account (with a display name) is ever left that no login reaches. What remains is the window inside that one statement.
    • Snapshots: one per ended year, activity, context and content version, for the period from 1 August of that year to the next 1 August (midnight in Oslo), with the configured k. aggregates holds the mappe's figures (MAPPE-002: participants, completion rate, median attempts, mean change) as activityAggregates computes them from that year's rows (by their stored year) under the mappe's group rules (context, version and semester; groups below k left out; D-095 and its amendment of 2026-11-04), with source: "yearly-purge", the year and suppressed; a hidden value is absent. They are written in one transaction under a PostgreSQL advisory lock, and not again for a year that has them. Insight's per-question cells are not kept: they describe at most a semester, which has ended. The mappe does not read the snapshots yet (open).
    • Dry run and log: a dry run counts, per table, the rows a real run would delete and the snapshots it would write, and changes nothing else. The job logs that plan, counts only, as the first line of every run.
    • Audit (DATA-007): every run, dry or real, from the job or the CLI, writes purge.run with target AcademicYear and the ended year, no actor (actorUserId null, as the schema has it for scheduled jobs; the CLI has no login), and the details trigger (job or cli), dryRun, outcome (completed or failed), years (the stored years the run covered) and counts. A run that fails writes its event with what it had done, then fails.
    • Idempotent: a second run finds nothing to delete and writes no snapshot, and is audited like any run; the job starts none once a completed real run for the ended year is audited.
    • The secret: when the job starts and after each completed real run, it logs a warning with the years (only the years) of the secrets in PSEUDONYM_SECRETS up to the latest ended year with a completed real run in the audit log (a run takes every stored year up to its own, so all those secrets are stale). The runbook (docs/ops/yearly-purge.md) gives the steps, the configuration change and how to check it.
    • H5PUserData's year: principalToH5pActor puts learnerKeyYearOf(principal, now) on the H5P actor (learnerKeyYear); the state route runs Lumi's write inside withLearnerKeyYear (h5p/storage/learnerStateYear.ts), and learnerStateWrites.ts sets academicYear on insert and on update, which for one key is always the key's year.

D-108 · Data-subject requests: a server CLI that HVL operations run

  • Context: DATA-008 asks for an admin-only tool that takes a Feide ID or an (iss, sub) pair, derives the learner keys for the retained academic years, and exports (JSON) or deletes that learner's data, with every use audited. Lumi 10.0.4's ContentUserDataManager.deleteAllContentUserDataByUser checks the permission for the user named but deletes the acting user's data (ContentUserDataManager.js:39-43, unchanged on Lumi's master, D-081). Such a request reaches HVL through its data protection officer, not through the app, and the identifiers it needs are exactly those the app never stores (DATA-002).
  • Decision:
    • Form: a CLI in apps/server (export, delete, and a dry run that counts), run by HVL operations where the server runs. No web page and no HTTP route.
    • Finding the learner: from the Feide ID and/or (iss, sub), in memory only, the CLI derives the learnerKey for every year in PSEUDONYM_SECRETS and the Identity.subjectHash for every key in IDENTITY_HASH_KEYS (D-055).
    • Scope: the learner's XapiStatement, H5PUserData and GradeSyncJob rows, their learner Identity rows and the learner User rows then left without one (D-034). H5PUserData is deleted through our own storage (h5p/storage/PrismaContentUserDataStorage.ts), never through Lumi's manager. k-suppressed snapshots hold no learner data and stay. The export is JSON with the stored fields, contexts as D-103's strings.
    • Audit: each run writes an audit event (export or deletion) with the counts. Its target is a random request ID, never the Feide ID, the sub or a learner key. The operator names their own HVL admin account (a Feide ID in ADMIN_FEIDE_IDS that has a staff account), which is recorded as the actor; nothing else about them is stored.
  • Alternatives considered: (a) An admin web page with a Feide admin session and the CSRF token: a page that accepts other people's Feide IDs and Canvas subjects over the web, for a rare task that the DPO's process brings to HVL operations anyway. (b) Lumi's deleteAllContentUserDataByUser: it deletes the wrong person's data.
  • Consequences: DATA-008's "admin-only" holds twice over: only operations can run the CLI, and only for an HVL admin. A staff member's own data (account, authored content, co-authorships) is outside the CLI; the runbook says how HVL handles such a request by hand until that is decided (open; HVL's DPO, Q6). The Lumi bug goes into the upstream drafts (D-112). The integration test exports and deletes a learner with rows in two academic years and checks that another learner's rows remain.
  • Amendment (2026-11-04, step 5, the CLI built): how apps/server/src/privacy/dsr/ carries this out; the runbook is docs/ops/data-subject-requests.md.
    • Commands: export and erase, each with --operator <feide-id>; erase is a dry run that counts unless it is given --confirm. Run from apps/server as npm run --silent privacy:dsr -- …. Exit codes: 0 done, 1 refused or failed, 2 usage or an unreadable data subject, 3 an erasure that found rows written while it ran.
    • The data subject on standard input: one JSON object, {"feideId": "…", "lti": [{"issuer": "…", "sub": "…"}]}, with at least one identifier; never in the arguments, which stay in the shell's history and show in the host's process list. The Feide ID is normalised as at login (D-054); iss and sub are taken exactly. A fault is named by its field, never by its value, and JSON.parse's own message, which can quote the input, is never shown.
    • Keys: for every year in PSEUDONYM_SECRETS and every identifier given, the learnerKey of feide|<id> and of each lti|<iss>|<sub> (D-011, DATA-002), and their Identity.subjectHash under every IDENTITY_HASH_KEYS key (D-055). A Feide ID finds no Canvas rows and a Canvas sub no portal rows, as they are different pseudonyms, so the runbook asks for both (Canvas's sub is the user's lti_id). The CLI refuses to start without the secrets, and names by year only the stored academic years that no configured secret covers (unreachableYears): no identifier can find their rows, which the yearly purge should have removed (D-107).
    • Operator: --operator must be in ADMIN_FEIDE_IDS and have a staff account through a Feide identity. Otherwise the run is refused before any learner row is read, and the refusal is audited without an actor.
    • Export: one JSON document on standard output, with a count summary on standard error: the request ID and moment, the years searched, each learnerKey with its year and variant, then the stored fields of the XapiStatement, H5PUserData and GradeSyncJob rows, each grade job's course as D-103's string. The encrypted sub is left out, and ltiSubStored says whether one is held: its plaintext is the sub the request gave, and the ciphertext is of no use to the person. It also lists the matched learner Identity and User rows and, beyond D-108's scope, the learner accounts' AuthAuditEvent rows (D-064: portal logins and logouts), which are data about the person too.
    • Erasure: in the purge's order (D-107's amendment of 2026-11-04): GradeSyncJob, XapiStatement, H5PUserData (through PrismaContentUserDataStorage.deleteAllContentUserDataByUser, one key at a time, with D-036's state view), the matched learner Identity rows, then the learner User rows left without an identity and owning no content. Each table goes in its own statements, not in one transaction (the storage takes the server's client), so a run that fails part-way is audited failed with what it deleted, and a second run deletes the rest. It then counts again: rows a learner wrote meanwhile (a portal session lasts up to 12 hours, D-057; an LTI request stops once its identity is gone) are printed as remaining, with exit code 3.
    • Not touched: staff accounts (counted as staffAccounts; D-108 leaves a staff member's own data to HVL by hand); the AuthAuditEvent rows, kept their 2 years for security (DATA-007): once the account is gone no identifier finds them, though their ipHash stays linkable to an IP address (HVL's DPO to confirm, Q6); and records that expire on their own: ltijs's ID tokens (24 hours, D-052), portal sessions (12 hours) and logs, which hold no personal data (DATA-009).
    • Audit (DATA-007): dataSubject.export or dataSubject.erase, target DataSubjectRequest with a random request ID (printed for HVL's case record, which alone links it to the person), the operator's User.id as actor (none for a refusal), and the details dryRun, outcome (completed, failed or refused), years, identifiers (how many Feide IDs and Canvas subjects were given), counts, unreachableYears and, after an erasure, remaining: numbers, years and fixed words, never an identifier, key or hash. The CLI writes no log lines. A run stopped by its arguments, an unreadable data subject or the configuration reads and writes nothing, so it is not audited.
  • Amendment (2026-11-05, step 5 review): gaps the review found, closed in apps/server/src/privacy/dsr/ and the runbook.
    • Interruption: once the data subject is read, SIGINT (Ctrl-C), SIGTERM and SIGHUP are held until the run has written its audit event; the first prints one note. By default each of them ended the process at once, so an erasure stopped by Ctrl-C, a closed SSH session or a container stop deleted rows with no audit event, against DATA-008's "every use is audited". SIGKILL, Ctrl-\ (SIGQUIT) and a crash cannot be held: such a run stays unaudited, a residual the runbook names.
    • Export only to a file or a pipe: export refuses, with exit code 2 and before standard input is read, when standard output is a terminal, so the person's record never lands in a terminal's scrollback or a recorded session by mistake.
    • Failures: a Prisma or driver error is printed by logging/prismaErrorSummary.ts's value-free line (its name and database code), any other error by its name and code, as before (DATA-009).
    • Staff accounts (staffAccounts) are accounts of kind staff: a staff member's, but also a student author's (D-059; the citation read D-089 until the integration of 2026-11-05) and that of someone Canvas launched as an author (LTI-004). The runbook tells operations to handle such an account by hand, as for a staff member, whoever the person is.
    • npm's debug log: npm writes the command line, and so the operator's own Feide ID (never the data subject's, which is on standard input), to ~/.npm/_logs even with --silent. The runbook's commands add --logs-max=0, which writes none (DATA-009).

D-109 · Database roles, encrypted-connection checks in production, and a request log without personal data

  • Context: DATA-010 asks for separate database roles for the app, for migrations and for read-only analytics, with the migration role used only in CI/CD; today one user, hvli, does everything (compose, .env.example, CI). DATA-004 asks for EEA hosting, TLS 1.2 or later and encryption at rest, verified by a deployment checklist in docs/ops/. config/productionChecks.ts already refuses some unsafe production settings (an http Feide issuer, PDF_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX), but not an unencrypted database, Redis or S3 connection. NFR-006 asks for structured logs with request ID, route, status and latency and no personal data; pino redacts by key (DATA-009), but there is no request log yet, and a raw URL can carry an ltik, a file grant or IDs.
  • Decision:
    • Roles: an SQL script creates hvli_migrator (owns the schema and runs prisma migrate deploy), hvli_app (reads and writes rows only, with default privileges for the tables the migrator adds later) and hvli_analytics (read-only, without the encrypted and token columns, which the script and the data inventory list). The server connects with DATABASE_URL (the app role); migrations use their own URL, set only in CI/CD and in the deployment's migrate step. Development and CI may keep one user; a test proves that the app role cannot change the schema. Creating the roles in production is a step for HVL's database administrator (Q5).
    • Production checks: in production the server refuses to start with a DATABASE_URL whose sslmode is not require or verify-full, a REDIS_URL that is redis:// rather than rediss://, or an http: S3_ENDPOINT. Residency in the EEA cannot be read from a setting: it stays a checklist item with the provider's facts (Q5), and the start-up log names the configured S3 region and the database and Redis hosts (never credentials), so the checklist can be ticked against them. If HVL's set-up protects a hop another way, the exception comes by amendment.
    • Request log (NFR-006): one structured line per response with a request ID (a well-formed inbound X-Request-Id, otherwise a random one, sent back in the response), the method, the matched route pattern (never the raw path or query), the status and the time taken in milliseconds. No user ID, IP address or body. The redaction key list (DATA-009) gains S6's keys (statement answers, the sub, client assertions and tokens).
  • Alternatives considered: (a) TLS as a checklist item only: a missing sslmode is easy to overlook and silently unencrypted. (b) Logging the URL with its query redacted: the path itself carries grants and IDs (/h5p/files/<grant>/…).
  • Consequences: docs/ops/ (the deployment checklist and the runbook) describes the roles, the second URL, the TLS settings and the 30-day log retention (DATA-009); .env.example documents the migration URL. The checklist recommends verify-full, since require encrypts without checking the server's certificate.
  • Amendment (2026-11-04, step 5, the roles, checks and request log built): what was built; the points marked narrowed or changes alter the decision above. The runbook is docs/ops/database-roles.md.
    • Roles, as two scripts: apps/server/prisma/roles/01-roles.sql, run once per database by HVL's database administrator (a superuser, or the database owner with CREATEROLE), creates the three roles if they are missing and resets their attributes (LOGIN, never superuser, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, replication or BYPASSRLS), takes every privilege on the database and on schema public from PUBLIC, gives the three roles CONNECT, gives hvli_migrator CREATE on the database and makes it the owner of public. 02-grants.sql, run as hvli_migrator after every prisma migrate deploy (it refuses any other user, because ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES binds to the user that runs it), grants the app its rows and builds the analytics views. Both are idempotent and hold no password: the administrator sets them with psql's \password (sent hashed) or uses certificates. A small runner, apps/server/src/infra/databaseRolesCli.ts roles|grants, runs one script in one transaction with the DATABASE_URL of that run (the administrator's, or the migration URL, as prisma migrate deploy reads it), and never prints the URL.
    • The app (narrowed): SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on every table in public, also on the tables later migrations add (default privileges), and sequences; nothing on Prisma's _prisma_migrations; and on the three audit tables (AuditEvent, AuthAuditEvent, LibraryAuditEvent) SELECT and INSERT only, so a flaw in the app cannot rewrite or erase the audit trail (DATA-007). Never TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER, CREATE or TEMPORARY. No server code updates or deletes audit rows today (a test scans for it); the two-year deletion of audit rows, when it is built, needs its own amendment and grant.
    • Analytics (narrowed): instead of "read-only, without the encrypted and token columns", hvli_analytics reads aggregate views only, and no table at all: it has no USAGE on public, USAGE on schema analytics, and SELECT on analytics.insight_snapshot, a view (owned by the migrator) of the InsightSnapshot rows, which are stored only after k-suppression (D-106, D-107), with the activity's content type and snake_case column names for R and Python. Its sessions start read-only (default_transaction_read_only). A new view is a new amendment and may show only aggregates already suppressed with k; 02-grants.sql re-creates the views after each migration, and a migration that changes a column a view reads drops that view first.
    • Storage location (changes "residency cannot be read from a setting"): in production the server also refuses storage outside an EEA allow-list in apps/server/src/config/storageResidency.ts. Without S3_ENDPOINT (AWS itself), S3_REGION must be an AWS region in the EEA: eu-north-1 (Stockholm), eu-west-1 (Ireland), eu-west-3 (Paris), eu-central-1 (Frankfurt), eu-south-1 (Milan) or eu-south-2 (Spain), not eu-west-2 (London) or eu-central-2 (Zurich), which are outside the EEA (verify). With S3_ENDPOINT, its host must be the S3 endpoint of one of those regions (s3.<region>.amazonaws.com, also s3.dualstack.…) or lie under an approved domain: hvl.no or sikt.no (verify, Q5). The lists are code, not an environment variable, because whoever sets S3_ENDPOINT would set the list as well; a reviewed change with an amendment here adds an entry. The check catches a wrong setting (a region outside the EEA, a test endpoint left in place); it proves nothing about where a server stands, which stays the checklist's evidence (Q5). Database and Redis hosts are usually internal names or addresses, so they are not judged by name: deploymentLocations(env) gives the database and Redis hosts, the S3 region and the S3 endpoint's host (never a user, password or path) for the start-up log line.
    • TLS, made exact: DATABASE_URL's sslmode may also be verify-ca (it encrypts and checks the certificate authority, more than require). Only sslmode counts, the parameter libpq tools read too; node-postgres's own ssl=true is not accepted. node-postgres 8.23 treats require and verify-ca as verify-full (and warns at start) unless the URL says uselibpqcompat=true; the checklist recommends verify-full. Messages name the variable, and the region or host for storage, never a URL.
    • Request log, made exact: apps/server/src/http/requestLog.ts, mounted first in createApp (after the proxy setting), so every response carries X-Request-Id, health checks included. An inbound X-Request-Id is kept only when it is a UUID or 32 hexadecimal digits (nginx's $request_id), lower-cased; anything else is replaced by a random UUID, so a client cannot write text of its choice (a name, a token) into the log. The ID is also in res.locals.requestId for error logs. route is the pattern of the last route Express matched, after the paths its routers are mounted at (/api and /content/:contentId give /api/content/:contentId), taken when the route matches; a response no route served (a static file, the 404 page, the web app) names its router's mount path with /*, or * at the top. Mount paths are static (a test scans the sources for a mount with parameters), so route holds no ID. One info line, msg: "request", when the response closes: requestId, method, route, status, durationMs (to 0.1 ms) and aborted: true when the client left first; no URL, query, header, cookie, body, user ID, IP address or learner value.
    • Verified by: apps/server/test/db/databaseRoles.int.test.ts (connects as each role to a throwaway database and proves the statements each may and may not run), auditAppendOnly.test.ts, apps/server/test/config/ connectionEncryption.test.ts and storageResidency.test.ts, apps/server/test/http/requestLog.test.ts and requestLog.int.test.ts (an LTI launch, a play and an xAPI batch through the whole app; no line holds the ltik, the learner's learnerKey or a path with the activity's ID).
  • Amendment (2026-11-05, step 5 review of the roles, checks and request log): five gaps found and closed; the points marked changes alter the amendment above.
    • The AWS SDK's own endpoint variables (changes the storage check): without an endpoint in its configuration, the AWS SDK for JavaScript (3.1155.0) sends S3 requests to AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3, else AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, else an endpoint_url in the shared AWS config file. Verified: with S3_ENDPOINT unset, S3_REGION=eu-north-1 and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3=http://…, the client sent to that http host, past both the TLS and the EEA checks. Production therefore refuses either variable when it is set (any value), naming the variable only: S3_ENDPOINT is the one setting for another store. productionProblems gets the raw environment for this (loadEnv passes its source). The shared config file is not in the environment: apps/server/src/infra/s3Client.ts should make the SDK ignore configured endpoints (an integrator item); until then the deployment checklist says no AWS config file is mounted. Added 2026-11-05 (integration): done. The client is built with the SDK's ignoreConfiguredEndpointUrls: true, so AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3, AWS_ENDPOINT_URL and a config file's endpoint_url are never read, in any mode, and S3_ENDPOINT still names the store (apps/server/test/infra/s3Client.test.ts, which fails without it). The production refusal of the two variables stays, so a mistaken setting is named at start-up rather than silently ignored. main.ts now writes the start-up line (deployment locations: the database and Redis hosts, the S3 region and endpoint host).
    • The migration URL's TLS (changes the runbook): Prisma 7.10.1's CLI (migrate deploy, db execute) does not honour sslmode=verify-full: it connected to a server whose certificate names another host. It checks the certificate and its host only with sslaccept=strict. node-postgres, which the grants runner uses, reads sslmode=require as verify-full. The migration URL is therefore …?sslmode=require&sslaccept=strict (plus sslrootcert=<CA file> when the CA is not in the system store): both tools then refuse a wrong certificate (verified against the local PostgreSQL with 127.0.0.1 for a localhost certificate). The server's DATABASE_URL keeps verify-full; its client is node-postgres.
    • Start-up facts: node-postgres connects to a host query parameter rather than the URL's host (pg-connection-string), so deploymentLocations names that host when the URL has one.
    • The role test: it sets the three cluster-wide roles' passwords to a published test value, so it refuses a database server other than this machine (localhost, a 127.x address, ::1 or a socket), where it would reset real roles' passwords.
    • Views down before each migration (changes "a migration that changes a column a view reads drops that view first"): once 02-grants.sql has built analytics.insight_snapshot, PostgreSQL refuses a migration that retypes or drops a column the view reads (verified: InsightSnapshot.k or H5PContent.mainLibrary to another type gives SQLSTATE 0A000, dropping InsightSnapshot.contextId gives 2BP01). The development database and CI have no views, so such a migration would fail first in a production deployment, and InsightSnapshot is a table the yearly purge (D-107) has just begun to write. A third script, apps/server/prisma/roles/00-views-down.sql, run as hvli_migrator (it refuses any other user) by the runner's views-down step right before prisma migrate deploy, drops every view in schema analytics and nothing else: no table, schema or grant. The grants step then builds the views again. The views hold no data; analysts miss them only during the deployment. The migrate step is views-down, prisma migrate deploy, grants.
  • Amendment (2026-11-05, the step-5 privacy and security review: bucket names): Found: the storage check judges S3_REGION and S3_ENDPOINT only, but the AWS SDK for JavaScript (3.1155.0) also routes by the bucket. Verified: with S3_ENDPOINT unset, S3_REGION=eu-north-1 and S3_CONTENT_BUCKET set to an S3 access point ARN of us-east-1, the client sent to <name>-<account>.s3-accesspoint.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, and an Outposts ARN of us-west-2 to …s3-outposts.us-west-2.amazonaws.com, without AWS_S3_USE_ARN_REGION and past the EEA check; ignoreConfiguredEndpointUrls does not change it. Decided (changes the storage check): in production S3_CONTENT_BUCKET and S3_TEMPORARY_BUCKET must each be a plain bucket name by S3's naming rules (3 to 63 lower-case letters, digits, dots and hyphens, beginning and ending with a letter or digit), so an ARN, which holds : and /, is refused; the message names the variable only, never the value (an ARN holds an account ID) (apps/server/src/config/storageResidency.ts, bucketNameProblems; test/config/storageResidency.test.ts). An access point alias (…-s3alias) is a plain name and goes through the client's own region.

D-110 · Deployment and operations design: runtime, image, compose, content types, files origin, ClamAV

  • Context: NFR-007 asks for Docker images and compose files for local and staging use; NFR-002 for daily backups and a tested restore; SEC-004 for a separate files origin in production (D-012, D-045); SEC-006 for ClamAV when CLAMAV_HOST is set; D-096 for Chromium with æ, ø and å in the image. Found while mapping:
    • npm start runs the server's TypeScript through tsx, a development dependency of the repository root, so the server cannot start from a production install (Evaluator Guide limitation 13). A bundle or a tsc emit would break at least nine import.meta.url anchors (SERVER_ROOT and WEB_APP_DIR among them).
    • The real content types come only from npm run h5p:fetch-libraries, which needs GitHub (D-078); apps/server/var/ is not committed, the seed folder holds only hashes (Q10), the Hub is out of reach (Q7), and HVL's hosts may have no GitHub access.
    • Chromium refuses its sandbox as root (D-096), and playwright-core 1.56.1 is made for one Chromium build.
    • @lumieducation/h5p-clamav-scanner 10.0.4 (GPL-3.0-or-later; it brings clamscan 2.4.x, MIT, and ts-deepmerge 7, ISC) answers NotScanned when ClamAV fails, and Lumi refuses an upload only on MalwareFound (ContentStorer.js, H5PEditor.js), so it fails open. It also reads CLAMSCAN_* and CLAMDSCAN_* environment variables, which override the options passed to it. clamd's default stream limit (25 MB) is below SEC-005's 50 MB.
    • A files origin would fail the DATA-011 tests, which count every other origin as third-party (apps/server/a11y/support/motionAndNetwork.ts).
    • Whether Docker runs in this environment is known only after probe P3.
  • Decision: a design that steps 1 and 6 build; what they find changes it by amendment.
    • Runtime: tsx (4.23.15, already pinned) becomes an exact-pinned runtime dependency of apps/server, and npm start keeps running the sources. A build step waits for a reason worth reworking the anchors.
    • Image: one multi-stage Dockerfile. The build stage installs everything, generates Prisma, builds the tokens, theme and web app, and fetches H5P core and editor with their hash checks (D-027). The runtime stage has production dependencies only, runs as a non-root user, and carries the Chromium that Playwright 1.56.1 pins, with fonts-liberation (or fonts HVL licenses) so that æ, ø and å embed (D-096); the sandbox runs on unprivileged user namespaces or a seccomp profile, whichever HVL's runtime allows (Q5). No secret is baked into an image.
    • Compose: the app, a migrate step (with D-109's migration role) and a seed step go under a compose profile app, so plain docker compose up -d still starts only the test services (D-023, CLAUDE.md §3). A smoke test starts the profile and checks health, a launch and a player page (NFR-007's Verify).
    • Content types: a bundle of the libraries D-078 pins, built with npm run h5p:fetch-libraries where GitHub is reachable, with a SHA-256 manifest kept in the repository. The seeder installs from the bundle and refuses any file whose hash differs. Committing the bundle itself waits for Q10.
    • Files origin (SEC-004): FILES_BASE_URL, which in production must be https and another host than PUBLIC_BASE_URL; by default files.<host>, as spec 02 §2 draws it. The player's signed content-file URLs (D-058) move there first; the editor's cookie-authenticated file route stays on the main origin until a later step. The files origin serves files only, with SEC-004's headers, no cookies and no ltik, and with CORS for the app origin and H5P's crossorigin setting, so captions (VTT) still load. The DATA-011 tests count the configured files origin as first-party, since it is ours (D-012), and the player page's policy (D-070) gains it in the directives that load content files (at least img-src and media-src), and nowhere else. A separate registrable domain would isolate more (a same-site subdomain still gets SameSite cookies sent with requests a file could start, although it cannot set our __Host- cookies and a file cannot run script under CSP: sandbox); the domain is HVL's choice (Q5).
    • ClamAV (SEC-006): when CLAMAV_HOST is set (with a port and a time limit), the scanner is registered in malwareScanners, which covers editor uploads and package imports alike. Our wrapper makes it fail closed: a NotScanned answer or a time-out refuses the upload with our own error, not "malware found". The scanner gets its options only from our checked configuration; the checklist says not to set CLAMSCAN_* or CLAMDSCAN_*, and that clamd's StreamMaxLength must be at least 50 MB. Signature updates are HVL's (runbook). The package is pinned at 10.0.4, the version that matches Lumi 10.0.4's scanner interface (D-112).
    • Backups and runbook (NFR-002): backup and restore scripts with a round-trip test on PostgreSQL 16, docs/ops/RUNBOOK.md and docs/ops/DEPLOYMENT-CHECKLIST.md. The real daily backups, their 30-day retention and the restore drill each semester are HVL's.
  • Alternatives considered: (a) A compiled server (a bundle or tsc output): every path anchor reworked, to save the in-memory compile at start-up. (b) Debian's Chromium package: the distribution's security updates, but its DevTools protocol can drift from playwright-core 1.56.1. (c) Our own clamd client instead of Lumi's scanner: no new dependency and explicit failure handling, but a SPEC-DEVIATION from SEC-006, which names the package; a wrapper gives the same handling. (d) The editor's files on the files origin at once: that needs a grant model for the editor's cookie-authenticated requests, while the player is where learners meet uploaded files.
  • Consequences: Limitation 13 closes when this is built. The runtime dependency changes (tsx moved, @lumieducation/h5p-clamav-scanner 10.0.4 with clamscan and ts-deepmerge) pass check:pins, check:licences and check:audit. Until the editor's file route moves, SEC-004's "in production, content files are served from a separate origin" holds for the player only: a SPEC-DEVIATION for the editor route (marked SPEC-DEVIATION: D-110), mitigated because every file keeps nosniff, the sandbox CSP and attachment for all but media (D-045). If Docker does not run here, the image and compose files are written here and GitHub CI runs them (D-113). HVL decides the runtime (a Docker host, Kubernetes or OpenShift), the sandbox settings, DNS and certificates (Q5).
  • Amendment (2026-10-30, probe P3): Docker works here (Docker 29.8.2 with BuildKit and compose 5.6.0: builds with network steps, compose with health checks, and Chromium's sandbox as a non-root user), and a second agent re-ran every decisive step. So one Dockerfile and one smoke script run both here and in GitHub CI, and the fallback above ("written here, and GitHub CI runs them") is not needed. What changes:
    • Base: the builder and runtime stages start from ubuntu:24.04@sha256:fe81560990fae86dc4743202b2cb4d3df98d0bcf949173cecef15ce1127ef852, with Node 24 copied from node:24-bookworm-slim@sha256:c86ecead9e55a5210ac1727de38a4ca840bf03dcaf34dc9749addbf383b1920c (/usr/local/bin/node and /usr/local/lib/node_modules, with links for npm and npx). That digest holds v24.22.2, this host v24.22.1 and .nvmrc says 24: the digest decides. Ubuntu, because apt works here only from archive.ubuntu.com (deb.debian.org is refused), playwright-core 1.56.1's install-deps targets it, CI runs ubuntu-24.04, and its libssl3 makes Prisma 7.10.1 install its OpenSSL 3 schema engine. Not used: Debian slim (no libssl, so Prisma falls back to its OpenSSL 1.1 engine with a warning, and apt cannot fix that here), Alpine, and mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.56.1-noble (Node 22.20.0, root, 3.68 GB).
    • Build: npm ci runs on the Ubuntu builder, with install scripts (the @prisma/engines postinstall fetches the schema engine from binaries.prisma.sh) and with the root package.json, whose allowScripts names prisma, @prisma/engines and esbuild at their pinned versions, so a bump of one changes allowScripts in the same commit. Network steps use the bridge network. The agent proxy's CA reaches them only as an optional BuildKit secret (RUN --mount=type=secret,id=proxy_ca,required=false, which sets NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS only when the file exists), passed here and never in CI; it never enters a layer (checked with docker history). apt uses plain HTTP and needs no CA. Not used: --network host with proxy build arguments, which breaks apt (the agent proxy answers 405 to plain HTTP).
    • Egress: a build fetches only from Ubuntu's archive (archive.ubuntu.com, security.ubuntu.com), registry.npmjs.org (every package in the lockfile resolves there) and binaries.prisma.sh, and in CI from Playwright's download host for Chromium. It never fetches GitHub repository content: GitHub is gated per repository for this session, raw.githubusercontent.com answering is not a sanctioned route, and testing GitHub from inside a container was refused as a containment escape. So the H5P core and editor, fetched and hash-checked on the host by npm run h5p:fetch-core (D-027), and the content-type bundle above come into the build as build contexts, and their hashes are checked again there; this replaces "fetches H5P core and editor" under Image. The owner is asked to confirm the bridge network's direct egress (Q21).
    • Chromium: full Chromium (chromium-1194, about 597 MB), not the headless shell (about 323 MB): SharedChromium's default chromium.executablePath() finds it, so no new setting is needed, and the image runs the binary the tests run (D-065). The browsers come from a stage pwbrowsers (FROM scratch), filled in CI by npx playwright-core@1.56.1 install chromium and replaced here by --build-context pwbrowsers=/opt/pw-browsers, since Playwright's download hosts are refused here. The host's headless_shell is never copied: it is a shell wrapper with an absolute path. The host's chrome binary changed after its install marker, so the smoke prints chrome --version and the binary's SHA-256, and an image built here can be compared with CI's.
    • Sandbox: the app runs as a non-root user (uid 10001), PDF_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX stays unset (D-096), and the app service gets security_opt: ['seccomp=<file>'] with Playwright's v1.56.1 seccomp profile vendored in the repository (utils/docker/seccomp_profile.json at tag v1.56.1, 12 997 bytes, SHA-256 cc3e61cabda6bbc1e53e54d27ba4d55a9d3be829b6dd1a596f4a7b31b1cc7849, Apache-2.0), with its source in a README beside it and a test of the hash. It is taken from that tag through git, the route D-027 and D-078 use, and checked against the hash; P3's copy came over raw.githubusercontent.com (see Egress) and is not committed. Under Docker's default profile Chromium stops with "No usable sandbox!", as root it refuses its sandbox, and seccomp=unconfined or SYS_ADMIN work but allow far more. This replaces "unprivileged user namespaces or a seccomp profile" under Image. Whether HVL's runtime allows a custom seccomp profile joins Q5; if it does not, PDF export needs a renderer container of its own, never --no-sandbox. CI keeps its kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0 step before the container smoke; whether AppArmor needs more there cannot be tested here.
    • Fonts: install-deps chromium, and fonts-dejavu-core named so the image does not depend on what install-deps brings; Chromium picks Liberation Sans, which embeds æ, ø and å. The smoke checks one PDF with pdftotext (the æ, ø and å text), pdffonts (embedded subsets), pdfinfo (tagged, A4) and the launch log (no "No usable sandbox", no --no-sandbox); poppler-utils run on the host or in CI, never in the image.
    • Compose: the app's stack (the app, the migrate and seed steps, and its own PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7 and S3 emulator) is a separate compose file with its own project name, not a profile app in docker-compose.yml: that file's services have no profile, so they start with any profile, and they publish 5432, 6379 and 5000, which the native services hold here ("address already in use", observed). The new file publishes only the app, on 127.0.0.1, reaches the other containers by service name, and pins every image by digest; docker-compose.yml keeps the test services for docker compose up -d (D-023), and it and CI's service containers take the same digests. SPEC-DEVIATION from NFR-007, the file name only: the app's local and staging stack is not in docker-compose.yml.
    • Docker Hub through a mirror here: the anonymous pull quota counts per address of a rotating egress pool and was used up on two of three addresses, so this sandbox's dockerd runs with --registry-mirror=https://mirror.gcr.io, which serves the same digests. Dockerfiles and compose files keep plain docker.io names pinned by digest, and scripts resolve images only through the daemon (docker pull, docker build), never with client-side registry calls (docker buildx imagetools inspect, docker manifest inspect), which bypass the mirror. CI needs no mirror.
    • dockerd here: it does not persist (PID 1 is Firecracker's process_api, with no systemd), so it is started by hand with the mirror flag. The smoke script starts no daemon: it checks docker info and stops with that instruction. The sandbox's extras (the CA secret and the browser build context) are passed only when HVLI_DOCKER_SANDBOX=1 is set, never because a path exists, so CI cannot pick them up by accident.
    • Disk: the image is about 2.2 GB, an npm ci stage about 1.7 GB and the build cache up to about 6 GB, against about 17 GB free here at rest (the probes reached 92 % use). The smoke script prints the free space before and after, ends with docker compose down -v, removes its own image tags and prunes only its own build cache (its own buildx builder), never docker builder prune -af or docker system prune, which would remove other sessions' cache. The stopped hvli-pg, hvli-redis and hvli-s3 containers and their volumes (2026-10-21) are left to the owner.
    • Load test (NFR-001, D-114): k6, as grafana/k6:2.3.0@sha256:2dd4756ec6e14e62778916e1eb850108e4b499304c02df56760fa0bdb0fba0b8 (AGPL-3.0, a separate program outside the npm tree), observed working against a local target on the host and bridge networks (p95 about 4 ms, no failed requests). Not Artillery: 2.0.34 adds about 463 MB and a second Playwright (1.62.1 beside the pinned 1.56.1), and its floating ranges already broke 2.0.30 ("Cannot find module '@smithy/node-config-provider'"). 2.3.0 rather than the 1.x line, because the scripts are new and it is the version tested; the image rather than the release binary, so one pinned digest serves here and in CI.
  • Amendment (2026-11-05, step 6: the files origin, SEC-004): decided before the code; it settles what Files origin above leaves open.
    • Setting: FILES_BASE_URL, an origin. Unset, it is files.<host> of PUBLIC_BASE_URL with the same scheme and port, so development gets http://files.localhost:3000 (Chromium and Firefox resolve every *.localhost name to the loopback, RFC 6761 §6.3; Node does not, so server tests name the files host in the Host header). A PUBLIC_BASE_URL whose host is an IP address has no files. name, so FILES_BASE_URL must then be set. In every environment the files host must differ from the app's host: a second port on the same host is refused, because a browser sends a host's cookies to all its ports (RFC 6265 §8.5). Production also requires https. The start stops with a message that names the variable, never its value.
    • One process, two host names: the server tells the origins apart by the request's host (req.hostname, so X-Forwarded-Host counts only behind TRUST_PROXY). A request for the files host goes to a files-only router right after the request log and the base headers, before the portal session, LTI, Feide, /api, /h5p and the web app, so nothing there reads a cookie, an ltik or a session, and nothing sets one. HVL's reverse proxy sends both names to the same upstream and passes Host on (deployment checklist). Not chosen: a second listener, which needs a second port in every deployment and gains nothing, since the files router reads no credential.
    • What the files origin serves: only GET and HEAD /h5p/files/<grant>/<contentId>/<file> with a player grant (purpose content-file-url, issued by the player render after the View check, D-058), and OPTIONS for a CORS preflight of those; everything else is 404. Every answer, refusals included, carries D-045's nosniff and sandbox policy, and files keep attachment for all but media and Cache-Control: private. Answers allow the app origin by CORS (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <PUBLIC_BASE_URL>, never credentials), and the player's integration sets H5P's crossorigin: 'anonymous': H5P then loads content files in CORS mode (H5P.setSource), and H5P.Video's captions (<track>), which a browser refuses from another origin without CORS, keep working.
    • The app origin no longer answers a player grant: /h5p/files/… there is 404 whatever the grant, with no redirect (every player render issues new URLs, and a redirect would make the app origin answer for grants and copy them into Location).
    • The editor stays on the app origin, as decided above, with a grant of its own: saved files at /h5p/editor-files/<grant>/<contentId>/<file> under a new purpose editor-file-url, issued only by the editor render after the Edit check, and fresh uploads at /h5p/uploads/… as before (D-069). A player grant opens nothing on the app origin, and an editor grant nothing on the files origin. Why the editor waits: H5P's image editor (scripts/h5peditor-image-popup.js, libs/cropper.js) draws a saved image into a canvas without crossorigin and exports it with toBlob, which a cross-origin image would refuse, so cropping and rotating would break. The code marks this SPEC-DEVIATION: D-110; it is mitigated by D-045's headers and because only people who may edit the activity get these URLs. The cookie-authenticated /h5p/content/:id/*file and /h5p/temp-files/*file stay (H5P's fallback when an integration names no contentUrl, e.g. a pasted file from another activity).
    • Page policy: the player pages (portal and Canvas) name the files origin in img-src and media-src only; the editor page's policy does not name it.
    • Lifetime and scope of a URL: D-058's grant lifetime stays (12 to 13 hours): a player page fetches files long after it opened (InteractiveBook chapters, video seeking), so a shorter grant would break long sessions. A grant opens the registered files of one activity, never another activity's: H5P appends each file's path to one contentUrl, so a grant per file would mean patching H5P Core.
    • Tests: the DATA-011 helper counts the configured files origin as first-party. Test beds that serve the H5P router alone on one loopback server (httpTestbed) keep relative file URLs and mount the player's file route themselves; the app test bed, the e2e set and the accessibility suite run the real split on files.localhost.
    • Residual: files.<host> is the same site as the app; a separate registrable domain (HVL's choice, Q5) would also keep SameSite cookies set with a Domain away from file requests (see Files origin above).
  • Amendment (2026-11-05, step 6: the image, the app stack and its smoke test, NFR-007, MAPPE-004): decided before the code, after the P3 amendment; what the smoke test measures is added at the end of this block.
    • Files: deploy/Dockerfile (with deploy/Dockerfile.dockerignore), deploy/compose.app.yml, deploy/seccomp/, deploy/smoke/ (the smoke script), tools/h5p-bundle/ (the content-type bundle) and .github/workflows/docker.yml, apart from ci.yml. The runbook is docs/ops/docker.md.
    • Stages: node (only the source of /usr/local/bin/node and npm), base (the Ubuntu digest with Node copied in), deps (npm ci with install scripts and the optional CA secret), build (prisma generate and npm run build: tokens, theme, web app), prod-deps, pwbrowsers-download and pwbrowsers (P3), the empty stages h5pcore and h5pbundle that the build contexts of the same names replace, inputs (their checks) and runtime. Only runtime is tagged.
    • Runtime dependencies (narrows Runtime for now): prod-deps is the npm ci tree after npm prune --omit=dev, plus tsx and the packages it needs, taken from the same tree before the prune (npm query '#tsx, #tsx *'), because tsx is still a development dependency of the repository root. Moving it to apps/server's dependencies, as Runtime decides, is a change to shared files left to the integrator; the copy is then a no-op. prisma stays in the pruned tree as @prisma/client's optional peer (devOptional in the lockfile), so the migrate step runs prisma migrate deploy from the same image, with the OpenSSL 3 schema engine the Ubuntu deps stage installed. The build fails if tsx, prisma or playwright-core is missing after it.
    • Runtime image: H5P core and editor and the bundle are copied only from inputs, after their checks. Chromium chromium-1194 lives in /ms-playwright (PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH), with install-deps chromium, fonts-dejavu-core and tini from Ubuntu's archive; poppler stays out. The code is owned by root and read-only to the app's user hvli (uid and gid 10001), who owns only the H5P library folder (a volume). tini is PID 1, so Chromium's exited children are reaped, and the command is node --import tsx src/server/main.ts, not npm, so SIGTERM reaches the server's own shutdown. NODE_ENV=production and WEB_APP=prod are the image's defaults.
    • Content types (narrows Content types and the P3 Egress point): tools/h5p-bundle builds the bundle from apps/server/var/h5p-real/packages (or another folder) into a folder of its own: exactly the ten types' packages, each matching the fetch's SHA256SUMS (a changed, missing or extra file is refused), copied with a SHA256SUMS the build stage inputs checks again and the seeder a third time. SECURITY: it also refuses a package that carries an environment variable whose name says secret (TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, API_KEY, ACCESS_KEY, PRIVATE_KEY, CREDENTIAL) with a value, and names the package, the file and the variable, never the value. Found while building it: H5P.AudioRecorder 1.0 and H5PEditor.AudioRecorder 1.0 (in the CoursePresentation and BranchingScenario packages) build with webpack's DefinePlugin({ 'process.env': JSON.stringify(process.env) }), so npm run h5p:fetch-libraries writes the build machine's whole environment into JavaScript the player sends to every learner; here that included a session token. The fix belongs to D-078's tools (build those libraries with a minimal environment) and upstream (D-112). Until the packages are reproducible across machines, which this also prevents, the SHA-256 list kept in the repository waits: the bundle carries the list its builder wrote after these checks, and the GitHub workflow fetches the libraries with a scrubbed environment (env -i with PATH and HOME) and a cache key of its own.
    • Seccomp profile: deploy/seccomp/playwright-v1.56.1.seccomp, fetched with git from https://github.com/microsoft/playwright tag v1.56.1 (commit 54c711571a37de525377e6f3d3608c3e029b1829), file utils/docker/seccomp_profile.json, byte for byte (12 997 bytes, SHA-256 as in the P3 amendment). The file name has no .json, so no formatter rewrites it; deploy/seccomp/README.md names the source, and a test checks the hash and that clone, setns and unshare are allowed.
    • The app stack (deploy/compose.app.yml, project hvli-app): PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7 and moto 5.1.16 by digest, no published ports; one-off services buckets (creates the two buckets in moto), migrate and seed (from the bundle, into the library volume); then app, on 127.0.0.1 only, with the seccomp profile, no-new-privileges, every capability dropped but SYS_CHROOT (see Measured below), a read-only root file system and tmpfs for /tmp, the user's home and Next.js's cache. The keys and secrets come from the environment and are never in the file; the smoke script makes random throwaway ones. This stack is local: it sets NODE_ENV=development, because the production checks rightly refuse its plain-HTTP database, Redis, S3 and public URL; staging sets production with TLS endpoints and D-109's two database URLs (runbook). Its public URL is http://localhost:<port>, so the files origin is files.localhost (amendment above).
    • The smoke script (deploy/smoke/dockerSmoke.sh): prints the free disk space; builds with its own buildx builder (docker-container driver, moby/buildkit:v0.33.1 by digest) and --loads the image; brings the stack up with up --wait; checks /healthz, the migration and a seeded content type (its library folder and audit row); renders a sample mappe through mappeHtml and the real PdfRenderer inside the app container with the sandbox on (the probe below), and checks the PDF on the host with pdftotext (æ ø å Æ Ø Å), pdffonts (every font embedded) and pdfinfo (Tagged: yes, A4); prints chrome --version and the binary's SHA-256; then down -v, removes its image tags and removes its builder with that builder's cache. A BuildKit container resolves images itself, not through the daemon, so with HVLI_DOCKER_SANDBOX=1 the builder gets the mirror and the proxy's CA in its own configuration (refines the P3 Docker Hub point); the CA secret and the pwbrowsers context are passed under the same flag, never because a path exists.
    • PDF availability probe (MAPPE-004): apps/server/src/learningDesign/mappe/pdf/pdfAvailability.ts starts Chromium with the export's own launch options, opens one offline context and page with JavaScript off, closes it, and logs one line with pdfAvailable, pdfSandbox and a reason code (ok, sandbox-off, no-browser, no-usable-sandbox, root-without-no-sandbox, launch-timeout, launch-failed, page-failed), never an error text or path; it never throws. pdfCheckCli.ts beside it runs the probe and prints one sample PDF for the smoke. Calling the probe once after the server listens is a line in main.ts, left to the integrator.
    • GitHub workflow (docker.yml): on pull requests and pushes to main: npm ci, h5p:fetch-core, the scrubbed library fetch, the bundle, poppler-utils, the AppArmor step of ci.yml, then the same smoke script without the sandbox flag, so Chromium comes from Playwright's download host and images from Docker Hub.
    • Measured here (2026-11-05, three runs on a snapshot of 5064a49 with this step's files, 4 vCPU):
      • Changes: Chromium's namespace sandbox also needs CAP_SYS_CHROOT in the container's bounding set. With every capability dropped the launch fails (Check failed: sys_chroot("/proc/self/fdinfo/") == 0, after the namespaces are made), and with --cap-drop ALL --cap-add SYS_CHROOT, the seccomp profile, no-new-privileges and a read-only root it prints. So the app, and only the app, adds back SYS_CHROOT (tools/deploy-check refuses any other added capability), the probe reports that failure as no-usable-sandbox, and Q5 gains it: OpenShift's restricted-v2 allows neither the profile nor the capability.
      • Passed (HVLI_DOCKER_SANDBOX=1 bash deploy/smoke/dockerSmoke.sh, 152 s with a cold builder): image build 105 s, image 2 776 MB; up --wait with the one-off steps 24 s; /healthz {"status":"ok"}; 7 of 7 migrations; 77 libraries and 77 seed audit rows from the 10 packages; the probe {pdfAvailable: true, pdfSandbox: true, reason: "ok"} as uid 10001; a 25 179-byte PDF with æ ø å Æ Ø Å — Lærar, øving, årsplan., LiberationSans-Bold and LiberationSerif embedded as subsets, Tagged: yes, A4; Chromium 141.0.7390.37, SHA-256 of the host cache's chrome dd794b4e31017bc184f872bb65f1d8e5a2986a896f09d559b903bd0eaf83144a (CI's CDN copy to be compared). Free disk went from 16 GB to 8.2 GB at the peak and back to 16 GB; no container, volume, image tag or build cache of the run was left, and moby/buildkit:v0.33.1 stays pulled for the next run.
      • The bundle here was built from packages repacked in the scratchpad after the two AudioRecorder libraries were rebuilt with env -i PATH HOME; the repository's apps/server/var/h5p-real packages are refused by the guard (CoursePresentation and BranchingScenario), as they should be.
      • Fixed in D-078's tools (2026-11-05, the step-5 follow-ups): tools/h5p-libraries/libraryBuild.mjs runs each library's npm run build with PATH (Node's own folder and the system folders), HOME (an empty folder of its own, made anew for each build) and NODE_ENV=production only, plus what npm itself sets for a script (npm_*, INIT_CWD, NODE, COLOR, EDITOR); npm ci --ignore-scripts keeps PATH, HOME and the proxy and CA variables it needs (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, npm's registry, cafile, proxy and userconfig settings), which never reach the build; the stamp's buildEnv version makes every cached build rebuild in place (git clean -ffdx after verifiedHead, no new checkout), and [H5P-003] tests prove that a build sees no other variable. Verified here: the two rebuilt AudioRecorder files now carry 28 variables, all npm's own and PATH, HOME and NODE_ENV (the old ones carried 111, tokens among them); the other 21 builds came out byte for byte the same; the bundle guard accepted the new packages and refused the old ones; the local library storage was re-seeded from the new ones. Residual for HVL: every .h5p package, library folder or library storage built or seeded before this fix, on any machine or from a CI cache, carries that machine's environment: rebuild and re-seed it, and rotate any token it held.
      • Follow-ups review (2026-11-05), decided before the code: "npm's own script variables" were not all npm's own. npm exports every setting that is not its default as npm_config_<name>, also those read from the Node install's global npmrc (<prefix>/etc/npmrc), which an administrator may have given a proxy with its password (https-proxy=http://user:password@…). A probe here with a planted global npmrc found its value in the build's environment, so AudioRecorder would have baked it in. The build therefore also gets npm_config_globalconfig, naming a file in its own empty HOME that never exists, so no global npmrc is read; the user npmrc was already out of reach. The recipe becomes buildEnv 3, and an [H5P-003] test runs a build under a Node whose global npmrc holds a planted proxy password. npm's built-in npmrc inside its own install folder is still read; it is part of npm, not of the machine's settings. Verified here: without the setting that test fails on the planted password; a full fetch rebuilt the 23 builds in place in 137 s, and only the two AudioRecorder files changed (still 28 variables, npm_config_globalconfig now inside the build's HOME), with them the CoursePresentation and BranchingScenario packages; the bundle guard accepted these, and the local library storage was re-seeded from them.

(1) The CA check read docker history, which shows instructions, never file contents; the smoke now searches every file of the image for the lines of the proxy CA bundle's own certificates (those that are not among the image's Node roots; a CA planted in a test image was found). (2) pdfSandbox: true only repeats the launch option; the smoke now also reads the kernel's view while a page renders (deploy/smoke/sandboxProof.mjs): every renderer must have a PID namespace of its own and Chromium's seccomp filter on top of the container's (measured here: 3 NSpid levels and 2 filters with the sandbox, 1 and 1 with --no-sandbox). (3) Nothing showed the built web app or H5P core served from the image; the smoke now fetches /hjelp (nn), one of its scripts and /h5p/core/js/h5p.js. A player page and a launch (Compose above) still need content and a platform, so they stay with the e2e suites. The guards: tools/deploy-check missed plural secret names (PSEUDONYM_SECRETS written in the compose file passed), a password in a URL other than DATABASE_URL, list-form environment, and privileged, unconfined or host namespaces on any service; the bundle guard missed this server's own key lists (URL_SIGNING_KEYS, DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS), _KEY and _AUTH names, single-quoted values and …_URL values with a password, and scanned only some text types. All of these are refused now, with tests. PRIVACY: only the stack turned off Prisma's usage report (CHECKPOINT_DISABLE); the image now sets it beside NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED, so a staging run of the same image and its prisma generate do not report either.
  • Amendment (2026-11-05, step 6: ClamAV, SEC-006): decided before the code; it settles what ClamAV above leaves open. Read in @lumieducation/h5p-clamav-scanner 10.0.4 and clamscan 2.4.0, and measured against clamav/clamav:1.4@sha256:8ad6197396974726c35d017e50aaaaf4b91745726a04faec8480c203edd98052 (ClamAV 1.4.6 with signatures 28171 in the image), pulled through the mirror in 7 s:
    • Found: Lumi's ClamAVScanner.create merges CLAMSCAN_* and CLAMDSCAN_* over the options passed to it and asks clamd for its version before it returns. Its scan reports every answer that is not "infected" as Clean, while clamscan gives no verdict (isInfected: null) for a reply it cannot read: an empty file (clamscan then never sends INSTREAM; measured), clamd's COMMAND READ TIMED OUT, a service that is not clamd, or a connection closed after clamscan's idle time-out with no reply. Wrapping only NotScanned would pass all of these as clean. clamscan's time-out is an idle time-out per socket, so a clamd that reads and never answers can hold an upload indefinitely, and by default it falls back to a local clamdscan or clamscan binary. ClamAV 1.4.6's StreamMaxLength is 100 MiB by default (measured; the 25 MB above is an older default); 30 MB and 60 MB streams were scanned, and a 110 MB stream was answered INSTREAM size limit exceeded. ERROR, which Lumi reports as NotScanned. EICAR comes back as Eicar-Test-Signature.
    • Adapter (apps/server/src/security/malware/): we build clamscan's client ourselves from our checked settings only (TCP or TLS to CLAMAV_HOST:CLAMAV_PORT, no local binary and no fallback to one, no connection test at start, never remove, quarantine or log files), and hand it to Lumi's ClamAVScanner through its constructor, which is private in TypeScript only (UPSTREAM:; create is not used, so the environment variables above are never read). Lumi's scan still turns the verdict into MalwareFound, Clean or NotScanned; a strict client between the two makes a missing verdict an error, so Lumi answers NotScanned. The scanner registered in malwareScanners (FailClosedMalwareScanner) refuses with our own RejectedUploadError: upload.file.malwareFound on a finding, upload.file.scanUnavailable on NotScanned, a thrown error or its own limit on the whole scan (CLAMAV_TIMEOUT_MS). Both are 400 with a translated message, which the H5P editor shows whatever the status. An empty file is clean without asking clamd. At most four scans run at once in one process, because a package import scans its files in parallel; the time limit counts the wait for a turn, and a turn ends only when clamscan has finished with its socket. clamscan 2.4.0 becomes an exact pin of its own (MIT, the version Lumi's ^2.4.0 resolves to) and @types/clamscan 2.4.1 a development one.
    • Logs: one warn line per refusal with a reason code (malware-found with the signature names, unreachable, timeout, tls, connection-lost, size-limit, no-verdict, scanner-error), never a file name, a path or text from clamd; one line at start says whether scanning is on. clamscan itself writes socket errors to stderr (console.error, Node's error text, no personal data; UPSTREAM:), and Lumi logs to its debug logger, which is silent unless DEBUG=h5p:* is set.
    • Configuration: CLAMAV_HOST (a host name or IP address), CLAMAV_PORT (3310), CLAMAV_TIMEOUT_MS (30 000; 1 000 to 600 000) and CLAMAV_TLS (false). With no host there is no scanner: the default in development and tests. Production refuses to start without CLAMAV_HOST unless CLAMAV_ALLOW_UNSCANNED_UPLOADS=true says so (for a pilot without ClamAV, docs/ops/clamav.md; the start then logs a warning), and every environment refuses the two together, so the override can never be read as "let files through when clamd is down". Every environment refuses a CLAMSCAN_* or CLAMDSCAN_* variable by name, since nothing reads it. Production requires CLAMAV_TLS=true unless the host is the loopback (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1, e.g. a sidecar), because uploaded files would cross the network in clear text (DATA-004); clamd has no TLS of its own, so HVL puts a TLS proxy in front of it (runbook). Messages name variables, never values.
    • Scope: both upload paths, editor uploads (H5PEditor.saveContentFile) and package imports (ContentStorer), through malwareScanners, before a file is stored; the editor-upload route still runs the sanitisers first for their reasons, so an SVG is scanned after sanitising. Library files in a package are not scanned (admins only, D-004; the seed bundle is hash-checked). Signature updates (freshclam) and clamd's limits stay HVL's (runbook).
    • Tests: a fake clamd that speaks INSTREAM (EICAR found, clean, no verdict, an error reply, an answer that never comes, a closed port, TLS against a plain clamd), the configuration rules, and both upload paths over HTTP; one more test runs against a real clamd only when CLAMAV_TEST_HOST is set (run here with the image above and freshclam off, so database.clamav.net was not needed).
    • Residual: after a time-out, clamscan's socket stays half-closed until clamd closes it (its ReadTimeout, 120 s by default), so a hung clamd holds at most four connections, and uploads meanwhile are refused at the time limit. If clamd's host vanishes from the network instead, the kernel ends those connections only after its TCP retransmissions give up (about 15 minutes on Linux); uploads are refused, never let through, meanwhile.
    • Skeptic review (2026-11-05), with its fixes: no fail-open path was found. Both upload paths reach the scanner (production builds the editor only in createH5pRuntime; package imports use ContentStorer's temporary-files path, which scans every referenced file before it is copied, and files the parameters do not reference are never stored); refusals leave no temporary file (the route's cleanup and PackageImporter's finally). Measured with a TLS endpoint here: with CLAMAV_TLS=true an untrusted certificate and a certificate for another name are refused (reason: "tls") and the endpoint receives no byte of the file; a trusted one is scanned. One test was missing: dropping the signature-name filter passed every test, so a fake clamd now answers a finding named like a person and a file, which must still be refused while the name stays out of the log. The UPSTREAM: mark for clamscan's console.error (Logs above) is now in clamdClient.ts, and the runbook says that files stored while no scanner was configured are never scanned later, and that DEBUG=h5p:* makes Lumi log file paths.
  • Amendment (2026-11-05, step 6: backups, restore and the runbook, NFR-002): decided before the code; it settles what Backups and runbook above leaves open. What the round-trip test measures is added at the end.
    • Files: tools/ops/ (the CLI backupCli.mjs and its modules, with tests), the runbook docs/ops/runbook.md (lower case, as the other runbooks in docs/ops/; it replaces the planned RUNBOOK.md), and the deployment checklist as a section of that runbook rather than a file of its own, so the start, the settings and the checklist are read together. Root scripts: ops:backup, ops:backup-verify, ops:restore.
    • What a backup holds: the database as pg_dump --format=custom (every table, _prisma_migrations and the analytics views) and the objects of the content bucket (S3_CONTENT_BUCKET). Not the temporary bucket: its files are editor uploads not yet saved, with a 1-day lifecycle; after a restore nothing refers to them, and a 30-day backup would keep them 30 times longer than the bucket does. Not the H5P library folder: the deployment's seed step installs the libraries again from the hash-checked bundle (the step-6 image amendment above); a library an administrator installed by hand needs that volume copied too (runbook).
    • Format: one folder hvli-backup-<UTC yyyymmddThhmmssZ> with database.dump, objects/<sha256> (each object stored once under its own hash, never under its key, so no key can name a path on restore), MANIFEST.json (format, time, the PostgreSQL major version, each table's row count, and each object's key, size, content type and SHA-256) and SHA256SUMS over every other file. It is written as a hidden .hvli-backup-….partial folder, renamed only when complete, and removed if the run fails. Folders are 0700 and files 0600.
    • Exact counts: the manifest's row counts are read from the dump itself (pg_restore --data-only to a stream, counting each table's COPY lines), so they describe exactly the snapshot pg_dump took, also while the server writes. Order: the database first, then the bucket, so an object added meanwhile is only an extra file; the restore reports H5PContentFile rows whose object is missing.
    • Restore: checks SHA256SUMS first (a changed, missing or extra file stops it and names the file), then refuses a target database that has any table or view in public or analytics, and a target bucket that holds any object, so it can never overwrite data; it then runs pg_restore --no-owner --no-privileges --single-transaction --exit-on-error, uploads the objects, and verifies: every table's count against the manifest, every object read back and hashed, and every content-file row's object present. It prints one JSON line and exits 1 on any difference. The grants come back with db:roles -- grants (D-109), as after a migration.
    • Who runs it, with which role: the same environment variables as the server (DATABASE_URL, the S3_* settings), so the CLI needs no settings of its own. A backup needs a role that can read every table, which hvli_app cannot (_prisma_migrations, D-109): it runs with the migration URL, or with a backup role holding pg_read_all_data if HVL's database administrator creates one (open for D-109's roles). A restore runs as hvli_migrator into a new database set up with 01-roles.sql.
    • SECURITY: the password reaches pg_dump, pg_restore and psql only as PGPASSWORD in their own environment, which holds nothing else of the caller's, never in arguments, output or the manifest; a database or S3 endpoint not on the loopback needs TLS that checks the server (sslmode=verify-full or verify-ca, an https endpoint), as in production (DATA-004, D-109); AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3 and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL are refused and the SDK's configured endpoints ignored, as in the server's client; the client tools and both servers must share one PostgreSQL major version (16), which the tool checks, because a newer pg_dump's output can fail on an older server. Messages name a variable or a file, never a value.
    • Retention: after a successful backup, --keep-days (default 30, NFR-002) removes older complete backups in the same folder, recognised by their exact name, and nothing else.
    • HVL's part (runbook): the daily schedule, an encrypted copy outside the server (in the EEA, DATA-004), the restore drill each semester with its log, and the managed database's own backups where HVL uses one. A backup holds pseudonymised learner rows; while a year's pseudonym secret exists, that year's backups can still be linked to people (docs/ops/yearly-purge.md, step 4).
    • Tests: tools/ops/test/ titled [NFR-002]: the round trip on the local services (a database migrated with the real migrations, seeded rows and objects, back up, wipe, restore, compare every table's count and an object's SHA-256), a tampered file refused, a non-empty target refused, and the connection and retention rules as unit tests. In CI it needs pg_dump and pg_restore 16 on the runner.
    • What the round trip measures (2026-11-05, built): tools/ops/test/backupRoundTrip.test.mjs migrates a database of its own with the real migrations (23 tables with _prisma_migrations), seeds six of them (250 XapiStatement rows, 40 H5PUserData rows, content-file rows naming two objects, one of 300 KiB and one with æ, ø and å in its key), backs up through the CLI, drops and re-creates the database and the bucket, restores, and finds every table's count equal and the image's SHA-256 unchanged; a dump with one byte changed is refused by verify and restore alike ("database.dump has changed") and nothing is written; a second restore into the filled database is refused; and no run printed the password, a URL or an object key, also when the server refused a wrong password. Two mutations (the upload skipped; each COPY line counted twice) each fail the round trip. The whole drill of the runbook ran once by hand on role-managed databases: a source deployed as the migrate step does (01-roles.sql, views-down, migrate deploy, grants), backed up with the migration role's sslmode=require&sslaccept=strict URL (read as libpq's verify-full), restored as hvli_migrator into a new database set up with 01-roles.sql and a new bucket ("ok":true, 23 tables, 0 differing), then grants: hvli_migrator owns every table and the view, hvli_app reads the rows, hvli_analytics reads its view. Added while building: a missing bucket is a named error (S3_CONTENT_BUCKET names does not exist), as is a missing PostgreSQL tool. The runbook is docs/ops/runbook.md, its section 9 the deployment checklist.
    • Skeptic review (2026-11-05), with its fixes: no row or object was lost, and no secret reached a dump, a manifest or the output; the round trip passes again. Found and fixed: (1) the restore's own checks were untested in the direction a drill depends on: with the table, object and content-file comparisons forced to 0 and the empty-bucket check removed, every test still passed. tools/ops/test/backupRestoreChecks.test.mjs now restores a copy whose manifest (its checksums made again) expects one more user, a larger object and no second object, and must report tablesDiffering, objectsDiffering and contentFilesMissing of 1 each, "ok":false and exit 1; and it refuses a bucket holding an object while the database is empty, writing no row. Each of the four mutations now fails a test. (2) A run stopped by SIGTERM, SIGKILL or a reboot left its hidden .hvli-backup-<time>.partial folder, with learner rows, for ever; a backup now also removes such a folder once it is a day old (stalePartials, counted in removedExpired), tested alone and through the CLI. (3) The runbook gave db:roles, privacy:purge and privacy:dsr as root scripts; they are the server's (npm run db:roles at the root fails with "Missing script"), so those steps now say "from apps/server". (4) The runbook's DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS rotation removed the old key 12 hours after step 2 (D-056, written before the grade jobs), but GradeSyncJob.ltiSubEncrypted keeps the key of the job's last result write until 30 days after the job stops (D-104), and a job whose key is gone fails as subject-unreadable; the runbook now says at least 31 days. D-056 and apps/server/.env.example still say 12 hours (for their owners). (5) The runbook's Redis row says what is lost with Redis (the sessions; the NRPS counts until the next launches). Residual: a content file deleted between the dump and the bucket copy is not in that backup, and the restore reports it as contentFilesMissing (runbook section 6, step 3).
